mainTopic: Biased witnesses and judges, how the court questions עדים and reaches a verdict, and when an admission of debt is binding, including the rule for a מסית.
overview: This amud finishes the story of מר עוקבא. He refused to judge his former in-laws, not because they were still relatives, but because they would not obey the ruling. The גמרא then explains the משנה's 'friend' and 'enemy' who cannot testify. A groomsman counts as a friend for a limited time. The enemy rule comes from a פסוק, the friend rule from סברא, and the רבנן use the same פסוק for biased judges and for scholars who hate each other. A new משנה describes how עדים are questioned one at a time, how the judges vote and announce the verdict, and that a judge may not reveal he was outvoted. The גמרא discusses what words are used to scare the עדים, and that an admission of debt counts only when it is made deliberately before witnesses. A borrower who says 'I was teasing you' is exempt, though the court will not raise that claim for him. In capital cases the court argues for the defendant, except for a מסית, as learned from a פסוק and from the snake in גן עדן. This leads to the lesson that whoever adds ends up subtracting. אביי then begins to limit the 'teasing' rule, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Former relatives come to מר עוקבא, and he refuses to judge them
steps.stepSummary: The men were once relatives of מר עוקבא but no longer were. They came to him for a court case, and he told them he was disqualified from judging them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They had been relatives but were no longer related. They came before him for a court case. He said to them: I am disqualified from judging you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story. מר עוקבא refuses to judge men who used to be his relatives. This sets up the question that comes next: why is he refusing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה discussed relatives who 'became distant', meaning the marriage that connected them ended. These men are exactly that kind of case. So מר עוקבא's refusal looks like he holds they still count as relatives.

keyTerms.meaning: Relatives who became distant: people once related through a marriage that has since ended.
Before him.
A court case or judgment.
I am disqualified.

phrases.english: They had been relatives and became unrelated.
They came before him for a court case.
He said to them: I am disqualified from judging you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of מר עוקבא begun just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא declares himself disqualified from judging his former relatives.

steps.title: The litigants challenge him: the הלכה is not like רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The men ask whether he is following רבי יהודה. If so, they say they can bring a letter from ארץ ישראל showing that the הלכה is not like רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What is your reasoning? Are you following רבי יהודה? We will bring a letter from the West saying that the הלכה is not like רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The men push back on his refusal. They argue that it rests on a view that is not the accepted הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that if there are children from the marriage, the former relatives still count as relatives. Since מר עוקבא had children, refusing on that basis would match רבי יהודה. The men attack this by showing that the רבנן's view is the accepted הלכה, and under it they are not relatives at all.

keyTerms.meaning: What is your reasoning?
A letter.
'The West': ארץ ישראל, as seen from בבל.
The accepted ruling in practice.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the men think they are still relatives. They are actually arguing that they are not relatives, so that he should be allowed to judge them.

phrases.english: They said to him: What is your reasoning?
Are you following Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: In the משנה, רבי יהודה says that if there are children from the marriage, the in-law still counts as a relative.

phrases.english: We will bring a letter from the West
saying that the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מַאי דַּעְתָּיךְ? כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning behind מר עוקבא's refusal in step 1.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he is relying on רבי יהודה's view, it is not the accepted הלכה. So under the accepted view they are not relatives, and he may judge them.

steps.title: מר עוקבא explains his real reason: they won't obey the ruling
steps.stepSummary: מר עוקבא answers that he is not clinging to them as relatives. He is stepping away only because they will not obey the court's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Do you think I am stuck to you with a measure of wax? I am not saying that I am disqualified from judging you for that reason, but because you do not obey the judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: מר עוקבא agrees that they are not relatives. He gives a completely different reason for refusing to judge them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'wax' line means: I am not glued to you as family. So the challenge from רבי יהודה's view falls away. His refusal is not about being a relative at all. It is about not wanting to judge people who will ignore the verdict.

keyTerms.meaning: Do you think? Used to introduce a rhetorical question.
A קב (a measure) of wax.
I am stuck or attached.
You obey or listen.

steps.whatToRemember: The story is not proof that the הלכה follows רבי יהודה. מר עוקבא agreed the former relatives were not disqualified. He refused only because the men would not accept the verdict.
steps.whyThisMatters: This removes the story as possible support for רבי יהודה, and leaves the accepted view in place.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אַטּוּ בְּקַבָּא דְקִירָא אִידְּבַקְנָא בְּכוּ?
phrases.english: He said to them: Do you think I am stuck to you with a kav of wax?
phrases.notes: He means: I am not glued to you as family. I agree we are not relatives.

phrases.english: For I am not saying 'I am disqualified from judging you' for that reason,
but rather because you do not obey the judgment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אַטּוּ בְּקַבָּא דְקִירָא אִידְּבַקְנָא בְּכוּ?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the reason: the refusal had nothing to do with family relation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The men assumed he refused because he followed רבי יהודה and still counted them as relatives.
steps.terutzMaskana: He agrees they are not relatives. He refuses only because they will not obey the ruling.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: a 'friend' means a groomsman
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה. It defines the 'friend' who cannot testify as one's groomsman.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A friend: this is his groomsman,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It quotes the משנה's words about a friend or enemy being disqualified, which sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה disqualifies a friend or an enemy of a litigant from testifying. The משנה defines 'friend' as one's groomsman. Quoting this line opens a new section of analysis.

keyTerms.meaning: A friend, literally 'one who loves'.
His groomsman: his close companion at his wedding.
And so on: the quote continues in the משנה.

phrases.english: 'A friend: this is his groomsman,' and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the מר עוקבא story and opens a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the משנה, a 'friend' who is disqualified from testifying is one's groomsman.

steps.title: How long is the groomsman disqualified?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for how long a שושבין remains disqualified from testifying.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for how long?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just learned that a groomsman counts as a 'friend' who cannot testify, and now it asks how long that lasts. This one-word question sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being a groomsman creates a special closeness, but closeness from one event may fade. So the גמרא wants to know when the groomsman goes back to being an ordinary, valid witness.

keyTerms.meaning: And how much? Here it means: for how long?
Groomsman, the close friend who helps at the wedding

phrases.english: And for how long?
phrases.notes: He means: for how long is the groomsman from the last step disqualified?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how long the groomsman disqualification from step 4 lasts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long a שושבין stays disqualified from testifying.

steps.title: רב: all seven days of the wedding feast
steps.stepSummary: רב, through a chain of transmitters, says the groomsman is disqualified for all seven days of the wedding celebration.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא says in the name of רבי ירמיה, who says in the name of רב: all seven days of the feast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first answer: the groomsman is disqualified for the whole week of שבע ברכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב, the special closeness lasts as long as the wedding celebration does. Once the seven days of feasting are over, he can testify again.

keyTerms.meaning: The seven days of wedding feasting

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said
that Rabbi Yirmeya said that Rav said:
All seven days of the feast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The groomsman is disqualified for all seven days of the wedding feast.

steps.title: רבא: only the wedding day itself
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן, in the name of רבא, say that from the first day after the wedding he is no longer disqualified.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן say in the name of רבא: even from the first day and onward he may testify.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, shorter opinion: the groomsman is disqualified only on the wedding day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא holds the closeness is tied to the wedding day itself, not the whole week. So already from the day after the wedding he is a valid witness again. This argues with רב's answer in step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of
And onward

steps.confusionAlert: 'Even from the first day and onward' does not mean he is disqualified starting from the first day. It means that already from the first day after the wedding he is allowed to testify again.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say in the name of Rava:
Even from the first day and onward.
phrases.notes: From the first day after the wedding he can already testify; only the wedding day itself counts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to step 5, arguing with רב in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The groomsman is disqualified only on the wedding day itself.

steps.title: The enemy: source from the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a שונא, and a ברייתא learns from a פסוק that a non-enemy may testify and one who does not seek harm may judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'An enemy, anyone who has not spoken to him...' The רבנן taught: 'And he was not his enemy': he may testify about him. 'And did not seek his harm': he may judge him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next part of the משנה, the שונא, and brings a ברייתא with a פסוק as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא splits the פסוק into two halves. 'Not his enemy' teaches who may be a witness, and 'not seeking his harm' teaches who may be a judge. So an enemy is disqualified from both roles.

keyTerms.meaning: An enemy, someone who hates the other person
He may testify about him
He may judge him

phrases.english: An enemy: anyone who has not spoken, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: he has not spoken to him for three days out of hatred.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And he was not his enemy": he may testify about him,
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:23

phrases.english: "And did not seek his harm": he may judge him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next term in the משנה, after the discussion of the groomsman.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An enemy may not testify or judge, learned from the two halves of the פסוק in במדבר.

steps.title: Where do we learn that a friend is disqualified?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק covers an enemy, so the גמרא asks for the source that an אוהב is also disqualified.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have found a source for an enemy. From where do we know a friend?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the פסוק only spoke about an enemy, and asks what source teaches that a close friend is also disqualified. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה disqualifies both a friend and an enemy, but the פסוק just quoted only mentions an enemy. So we still need a source for the friend.

keyTerms.meaning: We have found (a source)
A close friend, someone who loves him
From where do we know?

phrases.english: We have found a source for an enemy;
a friend, from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Notes that the source in step 8 covers only an enemy and asks for a source for a friend.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the פסוק that an אוהב is disqualified.

steps.title: Read the פסוק as including the friend too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says to read the פסוק as also saying 'not his friend' and 'not seeking his good,' which disqualifies an אוהב as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: Read it this way: 'He is not his enemy and not his friend': he may testify about him. 'He does not seek his harm and not his good': he may judge him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we understand the פסוק as if it also mentions a friend, so a friend is disqualified the same way as an enemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that a witness or judge must be neutral, leaning neither against the person nor for him. So the פסוק is read as covering both sides: no hatred and no love, no wish for harm and no wish for good.

keyTerms.meaning: Read it this way (understand the פסוק like this)
His good, his benefit

steps.whatToRemember: For now, the גמרא reads the פסוק as covering both an enemy and a friend. The next step challenges this reading, and step 12 concludes that the friend rule really comes from סברא.

phrases.english: Read it like this:
phrases.notes: The words about the friend are not actually written; the גמרא is telling us to understand the פסוק as if they were.

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא לֹא אוֹיֵב לוֹ וְלֹא אוֹהֵב לוֹ – יְעִידֶנּוּ,
phrases.english: And he is not his enemy and not his friend: he may testify about him,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא מְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ וְלֹא טוֹבָתוֹ – יְדִינֶנּוּ.
phrases.english: and he does not seek his harm and not his good: he may judge him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 by reading the פסוק from step 8 more broadly.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק is read as also excluding a friend and someone who seeks the person's good, so an אוהב is disqualified from testifying and judging.

steps.title: Is 'friend' really written in the verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading from step 10: the word אוהב does not actually appear in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is the word 'one who loves' actually written in the verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on what it just said. The פסוק only talks about an enemy, so how can we read a 'friend' into it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 10 the גמרא said to read the פסוק as if it also says 'not his friend.' Now it points out that this word simply is not there. So the source for disqualifying an אוהב needs to be explained some other way.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written? A way of saying the word is not actually in the text.
One who loves; a close friend of one of the sides.

phrases.english: Is 'one who loves' written in the verse?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading offered in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 10 that the פסוק can be read as including an אוהב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word אוהב does not appear anywhere in the פסוק, so it cannot be the direct source.

steps.title: Disqualifying a friend comes from logic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the rule for an אוהב is based on סברא: an enemy is distant from the person, and a friend is close to him, so both are biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is logical reasoning. Why is an enemy disqualified? Because he feels distant from that person. A friend too: he feels close to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own challenge. It says the rule about an אוהב is not written in the פסוק but comes from logic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אויב is disqualified because his feelings push him against the person. By the same logic, an אוהב's feelings pull him toward the person. Either way his judgment is bent, so the reason behind the enemy rule also covers a friend.

keyTerms.meaning: Logical reasoning, as opposed to a source in a פסוק.
Enemy.
His mind is distant; he feels dislike toward the person.
His mind is close; he feels attached to the person.

steps.whatToRemember: An enemy and a friend are disqualified for the same reason: both have personal feelings that can bend their judgment. The enemy rule comes from the פסוק, and the friend rule comes from סברא.

phrases.english: Rather, it is logical reasoning.
An enemy, what is the reason he is disqualified?
Because his mind is distant from that person.
A friend too: his mind is close to that person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 11 by moving the source from the פסוק to logic.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the source: the rule comes from סברא, not from the words of the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The disqualification of an אוהב is read directly into the פסוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: The disqualification of an אוהב comes from the same reasoning that disqualifies an אויב: personal bias.

steps.title: What do the Rabbis learn from this verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן, who do not agree with רבי יהודה, learn from the פסוק ״לא אויב לו ולא מבקש רעתו״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis, what do they learn from this verse, 'not his enemy and not seeking his harm'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the other side of the debate. It asks how the רבנן use this פסוק, since they do not use it the way רבי יהודה does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes every פסוק teaches something. Since the רבנן do not agree with רבי יהודה's rule about a friend and an enemy as witnesses, the גמרא wants to know what lesson they take from these words.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis; here, the חכמים who disagree with רבי יהודה.
What do they learn from it?
One who seeks his harm.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי ״לֹא אוֹיֵב לוֹ וְלֹא מְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ״
phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this verse 'not his enemy and not seeking his harm'
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:23

phrases.english: What do they learn from it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי ״לֹא אוֹיֵב לוֹ וְלֹא מְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ״ מַאי דָּרְשִׁי בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from רבי יהודה's view to the view of the רבנן on the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from the פסוק, since they do not use it to disqualify an enemy as a witness.

steps.title: One part teaches about a judge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that one part of the פסוק teaches that a biased דיין is disqualified.
steps.simpleTranslation: One part is for a judge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer. One half of the פסוק is used for the rule about a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has two parts: 'not his enemy' and 'not seeking his harm.' The רבנן use one part to teach that a דיין who loves or hates one of the sides may not judge. The second part is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: One; here, one of the two parts of the פסוק.
A judge.

phrases.english: One part is for a judge.
phrases.notes: He means one of the two halves of the פסוק. It teaches that a judge who loves or hates a side is disqualified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first part of the answer to step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One part of the פסוק teaches that a biased דיין is disqualified, which the רבנן agree to.

steps.title: The other part: two scholars who hate each other
steps.stepSummary: The other part of the פסוק is learned like the ברייתא of רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה: two תלמידי חכמים who hate each other may not sit in judgment together.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other part is like what is taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי son of רבי יהודה said, 'And he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm.' From here we learn that two Torah scholars who hate each other may not sit in judgment together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer. The second part of the פסוק teaches that two scholars who hate each other cannot judge together on the same בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 was about a judge's feelings toward a side in the case. This step adds a new kind of bias: hatred between the judges themselves. So the רבנן still find two separate lessons in the פסוק, even though they do not learn the witness rule from it.

keyTerms.meaning: The other one; here, the other part of the פסוק.
As is taught in a ברייתא.
Torah scholars.
Sit in judgment together, on the same בית דין.

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן learn two rules from ״לא אויב לו ולא מבקש רעתו״: a biased judge is disqualified, and two scholars who hate each other may not judge together.

phrases.english: The other part is as it is taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says:

phrases.aramaic: ״וְהוּא לֹא אוֹיֵב לוֹ וְלֹא מְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ״ –
phrases.english: 'And he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm':
From here we learn about two Torah scholars
who hate each other,
that they may not sit in judgment together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second part of the answer begun in step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second part of the פסוק teaches, following רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, that two תלמידי חכמים who hate each other may not sit together on a בית דין.

steps.title: How the court begins examining the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The משנה opens a new topic: the procedure for examining עדים. They are brought into a room, warned, everyone else is sent out, and only the eldest עד stays to be questioned first.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: How do they examine the witnesses? They bring them into a room and warn them sternly. They send everyone else outside, and they keep only the eldest of the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins here and lays out the first stage of questioning עדים: who is in the room and who is sent out. This sets up the questioning that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each detail protects the truth of the testimony. The warning pushes the עדים to be honest. Sending everyone out means the second עד cannot hear what the first one said. Starting with the eldest gives an orderly way to question them one at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין: 'our משנה.' It marks the start of a new משנה.
Examine, check (the עדים' testimony)
They warn sternly, intimidate (so the עדים speak the truth)
They leave behind, keep (in the room)
The eldest (or most important) among them

phrases.english: MISHNA:
How do they examine the witnesses?
They would bring them into a room,
and warn them sternly,
and they send all the people outside,
and they keep only the eldest among them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It moves from the topic of which דיינים and עדים are disqualified to the actual procedure for examining עדים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עדים are brought into a room and warned. Everyone else is sent out, and the eldest עד is kept to testify first.

steps.title: What counts as valid testimony about a debt
steps.stepSummary: The first עד is asked how he knows about the debt. Secondhand reports, even from the borrower himself, are worthless. Only testimony that the borrower admitted the debt in front of the עדים is accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say to him: Tell us, how do you know that this man owes that man? If he says, 'He told me, I owe him,' or 'So-and-so told me that he owes him,' he has said nothing. His testimony counts only if he says: 'In our presence he admitted to him that he owes him two hundred זוז.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה shows what question the דיינים ask the first עד. It then explains which answers count and which do not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה contrasts two kinds of answers. Hearing about the debt, whether from the borrower or from a third person, is not enough. The עד must say the borrower admitted the debt directly to the lender in front of the עדים. The words 'בפנינו' are the key point.

keyTerms.meaning: He has said nothing: his words have no legal value
So-and-so, some person
In our presence
Admitted, acknowledged (the debt)
A silver coin (a דינר)

steps.confusionAlert: Even the borrower's own words 'I owe him' are not enough if he only said them to the עד. The admission has to be made to the lender in front of the עדים.

phrases.english: And they say to him: Tell us,
how do you know
that this one owes that one?
If he said: 'He said to me
phrases.notes: 'He' is the borrower himself, telling the עד privately.

phrases.english: that I owe him,'
or 'So-and-so said to me
that he owes him,'
he has said nothing,
unless he says:
'In our presence he admitted to him
that he owes him two hundred zuz.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאוֹמְרִים לוֹ: אֱמוֹר הֵיאַךְ אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the procedure: after setting up the room, the דיינים question the eldest עד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hearsay about a debt is invalid. Only an admission the borrower made to the lender in front of the עדים is accepted.

steps.title: Questioning the second witness and comparing their testimony
steps.stepSummary: The second עד is brought in and questioned the same way. If both testimonies match, the דיינים begin to discuss the case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Afterward they bring in the second witness and examine him. If their words are found to match, the judges discuss the matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes the questioning: the second עד is checked the same way. If the two match, the דיינים move on to discussing the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Questioning each עד separately lets the דיינים check whether the two stories match. Only after the testimony is confirmed do the דיינים start debating the verdict. This leads into the voting rules in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The second (עד)
Matching, consistent with each other
Literally 'carry and give': they discuss and debate

phrases.english: And afterward they bring in the second one,
and examine him.
If their words are found to match,
they discuss the matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the questioning process begun with the first עד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second עד is examined separately. If both testimonies match, the דיינים deliberate.

steps.title: The majority of judges decides the verdict
steps.stepSummary: With three דיינים, the verdict follows the majority. Two for זכאי against one for חייב means זכאי. Two for חייב against one for זכאי means חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If two say 'exempt' and one says 'liable,' he is exempt. If two say 'liable' and one says 'exempt,' he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains how the three דיינים reach a verdict when they disagree: the majority wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A money case has three דיינים, so a split is usually two against one. The two-to-one majority decides in either direction, whether to exempt or to obligate.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, not liable (wins the case)
Liable, must pay

phrases.english: If two say: Exempt,
and one says: Liable, he is exempt.
If two say: Liable,
and one says: Exempt, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁנַיִם אוֹמְרִים: זַכַּאי, וְאֶחָד אוֹמֵר: חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the deliberation from step 18 and gives the rule for reaching the verdict.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a three-דיין court, the two-to-one majority decides, whether for זכאי or for חייב.

steps.title: When one judge says 'I do not know,' more judges are added
steps.stepSummary: If one דיין says 'I do not know,' the court cannot rule, even if the other two agree. More דיינים must be added.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one says 'liable' and one says 'exempt,' or even if two say 'exempt' or two say 'liable,' and the remaining one says 'I do not know,' they must add more judges.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the last case: when one דיין cannot decide, the court adds more דיינים instead of ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'I do not know' covers all the cases here. A דיין who cannot decide is not counted, so only two voting דיינים remain. That is not enough, even if the two agree, so more דיינים are added.

keyTerms.meaning: I do not know (the דיין cannot decide)
They must add more דיינים
They rule him זכאי (exempt)
They rule him חייב (liable)

steps.whatToRemember: A money case has three דיינים and goes by majority. Testimony is valid only if the borrower admitted the debt in front of the עדים, and each עד is questioned separately. If any דיין says 'I do not know,' more דיינים are added, even if the other two agree.
steps.confusionAlert: It is easy to think two agreeing דיינים are already a majority of three. But the one who says 'I do not know' is not counted, so the court must still add דיינים.

phrases.english: If one says: Liable,
and one says: Exempt,
or even if two rule him exempt
or two rule him liable,
and one says: I do not know,
they must add judges.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶחָד אוֹמֵר: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ – יוֹסִיפוּ הַדַּיָּינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the exception to the majority rule of step 19: when a דיין abstains, there is no valid majority.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a verdict needs a full court of voting דיינים, not just two who agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If one דיין says 'I do not know,' the court adds דיינים, even if the other two agree.

steps.title: The senior judge announces the verdict
steps.stepSummary: Once the דיינים reach a decision, the בעלי דין are brought back in, and the greatest דיין announces who is זכאי and who is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the judges have finished deciding, they bring the litigants back in. The most senior judge says: 'So-and-so, you are exempt,' or 'So-and-so, you are liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה describes the final stage of the court case: bringing the parties back in and announcing the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, everyone else was sent out of the room while the דיינים discussed the case. Now the parties return. Only the outcome is announced, by one voice, the senior דיין, and not how each judge voted.

keyTerms.meaning: They finished the matter, meaning the judges reached a decision
The greatest or most senior of the judges
So-and-so, a placeholder for the person's name
Exempt (not obligated to pay) / liable (must pay)

phrases.english: They finished the matter,
they would bring them in.
phrases.notes: "Them" means the two sides of the case, who were sent out while the judges talked it over.

phrases.english: The greatest of the judges says:
So-and-so, you are exempt.
So-and-so, you are liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּמְרוּ אֶת הַדָּבָר, הָיוּ מַכְנִיסִין אוֹתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's procedure: after the vote (steps 19-20), the verdict is announced.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After deciding, the court brings in the parties and the senior דיין announces the verdict.

steps.title: A judge may not reveal that he was outvoted
steps.stepSummary: A דיין who leaves the court may not say 'I wanted to acquit, but my colleagues outvoted me.' The משנה brings two פסוקים showing that this is forbidden רכילות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that when a judge leaves, he may not say: 'I said exempt and my colleagues said liable, but what can I do, they outnumbered me'? About this it says: 'Do not go as a talebearer among your people,' and it also says: 'One who goes as a talebearer reveals secrets.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה teaches that a דיין must keep the court's discussion private and gives פסוקים as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verdict is announced as the court's single decision. If a judge reveals that he disagreed, he exposes a secret discussion and makes his colleagues look bad to the losing side. That is רכילות, and the second פסוק adds that it means revealing a secret.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where, asking for the source of a rule
They outnumbered me, meaning they were the majority against me
A talebearer, someone who carries stories from person to person
Reveals a secret

steps.whatToRemember: The verdict belongs to the whole court. A דיין may never tell people how the vote split.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that keeping the judges' discussion secret is a real איסור of רכילות, and not just good manners.

phrases.english: And from where [do we know] that when he leaves,
phrases.notes: "He" is one of the judges, after leaving the courtroom.

phrases.english: he should not say:
I declared exempt and my colleagues declared liable,
but what can I do,
since my colleagues outnumbered me?
About this it is said:
"You shall not go as a talebearer among your people,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:16

phrases.english: And it says:
"One who goes as a talebearer reveals secrets."
phrases.notes: משלי 11:13

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a rule about what happens after the verdict from step 21 is announced.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דיין may not reveal that he was in the minority. Doing so violates the איסור of רכילות.

steps.title: What words are used to warn the witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins by asking what exactly the court says to the עדים when it warns and frightens them, as the משנה mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: How do we speak to them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a question about the משנה's earlier instruction to warn the עדים. This sets up the next step, where an answer will be given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the עדים are warned (step 16) but did not say what words to use. The גמרא wants the actual wording.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
How? In what way?
We say to them

phrases.english: GEMARA: How do we speak to them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means the witnesses, whom the משנה said the judges warn before questioning (step 16).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the warning of the עדים mentioned at the start of this משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact words the court uses to frighten the עדים into telling the truth.

steps.title: רב יהודה: warn them that lying brings drought
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the court quotes a פסוק comparing a liar to clouds and wind that bring no rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: This is what we tell them: 'Clouds and wind, but no rain, so is a man who boasts of a false gift.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question by giving the wording: a פסוק warning that lying brings drought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links falsehood with rain being held back. The court hopes the fear of drought and lost blessing will stop the עדים from lying.

keyTerms.meaning: Clouds (rising vapors)
There is no rain
A false gift, used here for a lie

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
This is what we say to them:
"Clouds and wind, but there is no rain,
phrases.notes: משלי 25:14. The message to the witnesses is that lying holds back the rain.

phrases.english: [so is] a man who boasts of a false gift."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court tells the עדים the פסוק from משלי 25:14, warning that lies bring drought.

steps.title: רבא: a drought won't scare a craftsman
steps.stepSummary: רבא objects that עדים could brush off the drought warning with a folk saying: in seven years of famine, hunger never reached the craftsman's door.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: They can say, 'Seven years there was a famine, but it never passed by the craftsman's door.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רב יהודה's wording and argues that it will not frighten the עדים enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A drought threatens farmers. Someone who earns money from a trade still gets paid, so a lying witness who is not a farmer would not feel threatened. This means a stronger warning is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Seven years
Famine, hunger
At the craftsman's door
Did not pass by

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying that lying is fine or that the פסוק is wrong. He is only saying that this warning would not work well to scare the witnesses.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
They can say:
phrases.notes: "They" are the witnesses, saying this to themselves to shrug off the warning.

phrases.english: Seven years there was famine,
but at the craftsman's door it did not pass.
phrases.notes: A popular saying: someone who earns from a trade, not farming, doesn't go hungry in a drought.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to רב יהודה's answer in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's suggested warning, the drought פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The warning only scares farmers. Witnesses who are craftsmen would not care about drought, so the warning would not work to prevent lying.

steps.title: רבא's warning: a false witness is like a deadly weapon
steps.stepSummary: After rejecting the 'clouds and wind' warning, רבא suggests the court quote a פסוק comparing a false witness to a hammer, a sword and a sharp arrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: we tell them, 'A hammer, a sword and a sharp arrow is a man who testifies falsely against his neighbor.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא replaces the warning he just knocked down with a new one. Now the threat is personal danger to the liar himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The drought warning failed because a craftsman can always earn a living. So רבא picks a threat that hits the witness personally: a false witness is compared to deadly weapons, which implies he will die early.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, a sign that the earlier answer is dropped and a new one is offered
A hammer, something that smashes
A sharp arrow
A false witness

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said,
we say to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the עדים the court is warning.

phrases.english: "A hammer, and a sword, and a sharp arrow
phrases.notes: משלי 25:18

phrases.english: is a man who testifies against his neighbor as a false witness."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the warning that רבא rejected in step 25 with a new פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exactly does the court say to frighten עדים?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Quote the פסוק comparing a false witness to a hammer, sword and arrow, which threatens an early death.

steps.title: רב אשי: people believe no one dies before his time
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי objects that עדים can dismiss the death threat with a folk saying: even during seven years of plague, no one died before his time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to him: they can say, 'For seven years there was a plague, yet no one died before his time.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks רבא's warning the same way רבא attacked the first one: the עדים have a folk saying that makes the threat feel empty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's warning only works if the witness fears dying early. But if people believe each person's time to die is already set, a threat of early death will not scare them, so the warning fails.

keyTerms.meaning: They can say, meaning the witnesses could answer back
Seven years
A plague or deadly epidemic
Died (literally 'lay down')

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to him,
They can say:
For seven years there was a plague,
yet no person died before his time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי, יָכְלִי לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's warning from step 26, using the same kind of argument רבא used in step 25.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A threat of early death does not frighten someone who believes his time to die is already fixed, so the warning will not stop lying.

steps.title: False witnesses are despised even by those who hire them
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי, quoting נתן בר מר זוטרא, says the court tells עדים that liars are looked down on even by the people who hire them, proven from איזבל calling her hired witnesses 'worthless men'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: נתן בר מר זוטרא told me that we say to them: false witnesses are cheap even in the eyes of those who hire them, as it is written: 'Seat two worthless men opposite him, and let them testify against him, saying: You cursed God and the king.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the final answer: the warning is about shame and losing respect, not about punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both earlier warnings could be dismissed with a folk saying. Shame cannot be brushed off that way: even איזבל, who hired the witnesses against נבות, called them 'worthless men'. If the people who hire you despise you, everyone else surely will.

keyTerms.meaning: False witnesses
Those who hire them
Are cheap, worthless or looked down upon
Worthless, wicked people

steps.whatToRemember: The accepted warning to עדים is about disgrace: false witnesses are despised even by the people who hire them.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לִי נָתָן בַּר מָר זוּטְרָא,
phrases.english: Natan bar Mar Zutra said to me,
we say to them:
false witnesses are cheap even to those who hire them,
as it is written:
"And seat two men,
phrases.notes: מלכים א 21:10. These are איזבל's orders about the witnesses she hired against נבות.

phrases.english: worthless fellows, opposite him,
and let them testify against him, saying:
You cursed God and the king."
phrases.notes: 'Cursed' is written politely here as 'blessed'. That is how the פסוק avoids saying 'cursed God' outright.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אָמַר לִי נָתָן בַּר מָר זוּטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting רבא's warning in step 27, רב אשי offers a warning that cannot be dismissed with a folk saying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What warning will actually frighten עדים?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Tell them that false witnesses are disgraced even in the eyes of the people who hire them, as the פסוק about איזבל's hired witnesses shows.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The court frightens עדים with the shame of lying, not with threats of drought or early death.

steps.title: New section: a witness must say the borrower admitted in front of them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה: a witness who only says 'he told me he owes' is not enough, unless the witnesses say the borrower admitted in their presence that he owes 200 זוז.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he says, 'He told me, etc.', that is not enough, unless they say, 'In our presence he admitted to him that he owes him two hundred זוז.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה. This quote sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic changes from warning עדים to what counts as valid testimony about a debt. A witness who reports that the borrower told him privately is not enough. The witnesses must have seen the borrower admit the debt to the lender himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc., meaning the quote continues in the משנה
Unless they say
In front of us, in our presence
Admitted
Two hundred זוז, a sum of money

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument. The גמרא is just quoting the next part of the משנה so it can discuss it next.

phrases.english: If he said: "He said to me, etc."
Unless they say:
"In our presence he admitted to him
that he owes him two hundred zuz."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the topic of warning עדים and opens a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony about a debt is valid only if the witnesses say the borrower admitted it to the lender in their presence, not merely that he told the witness.

steps.title: The משנה supports רב יהודה: the borrower must say 'You are my witnesses'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה's rule supports רב יהודה in the name of רב: an admission only counts if the borrower tells the people present, 'You are my witnesses.'
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רב יהודה, who said in the name of רב: the borrower must say 'You are my witnesses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the משנה we just read backs up a ruling of רב יהודה. That ruling says a borrower's admission only counts if he tells the people present, 'You are my witnesses.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said 'he told me he owes' is not enough. The witnesses have to say he admitted the debt in front of them. The גמרא reads this as proof for רב יהודה: a casual remark is not a real admission unless the borrower deliberately makes the listeners into his witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: This supports him. It shows that a source backs up someone's opinion.
You are my witnesses. These are the words that turn a casual remark into an official admission.
An admission, here an admission that one owes money.

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the main rule for the rest of the section. An admission of debt has legal force only when the speaker clearly means it to serve as testimony.

phrases.english: This supports Rav Yehuda,
as Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
He needs to say, "You are my witnesses."
phrases.notes: 'He' is the borrower. He has to say this himself to the people listening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the משנה line quoted in step 29 supports רב יהודה's rule.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's ruling (in the name of רב) that the borrower must say 'אתם עדיי'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה, which requires that the borrower admitted 'in our presence' and does not accept a witness who only says 'he told me he owes'.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: someone who says 'I was joking' is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא quotes רבי יוחנן: if someone casually agrees that he owes a מנה and the next day says 'I was joking,' he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also said, by רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן: If one person says, 'You owe me a מנה,' and the other says, 'Yes,' and the next day the first says, 'Give it to me,' and the other answers, 'I was joking with you,' he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source that teaches the same idea. רבי יוחנן says a casual 'yes, I owe you' is not binding if the person later says he was only joking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds an actual case to the general rule. Because the 'yes' was said without making anyone his witnesses, he can explain it away as teasing. So he does not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated. This introduces an Amora's ruling that agrees with what was just said.
A sum of money equal to 100 זוז.
I was joking with you, or teasing you.
Exempt. He does not have to pay.

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
[If one said,] "I have a maneh in your hand,"
phrases.notes: This is a short way of saying 'you owe me a מנה.'

phrases.english: and he said to him, "Yes."
The next day he said to him, "Give it to me,"
and he said, "I was joking with you": he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a statement from an אמורא that agrees with רב יהודה's rule.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a casual admission without 'אתם עדיי' does not obligate the speaker.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of רבי יוחנן, as quoted by רבי חייא בר אבא.

steps.title: A ברייתא teaches the same 'I was joking' ruling
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same case: someone who agreed he owes a מנה and later says 'I was joking' is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also taught in a ברייתא: If one says, 'You owe me a מנה,' and the other says, 'Yes,' and the next day the first says, 'Give it to me,' and the other answers, 'I was joking with you,' he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third source, a ברייתא, that says the same thing word for word. It is setting up the ברייתא's next line, which goes even further.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the rule rests on a תנאי source and not only on אמוראים. The case is exactly like רבי יוחנן's. What is new comes next, in the 'ולא עוד' part of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way. This introduces a ברייתא that supports what was just said.
A teaching from the time of the תנאים that was not included in the משנה.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way [in a baraita]:
"I have a maneh in your hand," and he said to him, "Yes."
The next day he said to him, "Give it to me,"
and he said to him, "I was joking with you": he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's ruling with a ברייתא that says the same thing.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that someone who says 'I was joking' about a casual admission is exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with the identical case.

steps.title: He is exempt even when witnesses were hidden behind a fence
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא goes further. Even if witnesses were secretly hidden behind a fence and heard the admission, the man who later says 'I was joking' is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that. Even if the lender hid witnesses behind a fence and said, 'You owe me a מנה,' and the other said, 'Yes,' and then the lender asked, 'Would you admit it in front of so-and-so and so-and-so?' and he answered, 'I'm afraid you would force me to go to court,' and the next day the lender said, 'Give it to me,' and he answered, 'I was joking with you,' he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pushes the rule to an extreme case. Witnesses actually heard him say he owes, but he did not know they were there. He is still exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think real עדים who heard the admission would make it binding. But he never said 'אתם עדיי', and he even refused to admit in front of witnesses, so his words were never meant as testimony. They can be explained as just calming the lender down. This is the strongest support for רב יהודה's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but... This introduces a bigger, more surprising case.
He hid (the witnesses) in a secret place.
Behind a fence.
So-and-so and so-and-so. A way of naming people without saying who they are.
You will force me to go to court.

steps.whatToRemember: An admission of debt only binds a person if he meant it as testimony, by saying 'אתם עדיי'. A casual 'yes' can be taken back with 'I was joking,' even if hidden witnesses heard it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the hidden witnesses make the admission binding just because they really heard it. What matters is whether the borrower meant to admit before witnesses, and here he clearly did not.

phrases.english: And not only that, but

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ הִכְמִין לוֹ עֵדִים אֲחוֹרֵי גָּדֵר,
phrases.english: even if he hid witnesses for him behind a fence,
phrases.notes: The lender hid them so the borrower would not know anyone was listening.

phrases.english: and said to him, "I have a maneh in your hand,"
and he said to him, "Yes."
[He asked:] "Would you like to admit it in front of so-and-so and so-and-so?"
He said to him, "I am afraid
that you might force me into court."
The next day he said to him, "Give it to me,"
and he said to him, "I was joking with you": he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ הִכְמִין לוֹ עֵדִים אֲחוֹרֵי גָּדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and pushes its ruling to a bigger case: hidden witnesses who heard the admission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even when hidden witnesses heard the admission, the borrower is exempt if he says 'I was joking,' because he never meant his words as testimony.

steps.title: The court does not argue on behalf of a מסית
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: judges do not raise claims on behalf of a מסית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we do not raise claims on behalf of a מסית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last line of the ברייתא from the previous steps. This sets up the next move, because the line seems to come out of nowhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the ברייתא was about a man who admitted a debt and later said 'I was joking.' Suddenly it mentions a מסית, a person who tries to convince others to worship idols. The jump to a totally different topic is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: We raise an argument (for someone)
A person who tries to convince others to worship idols

phrases.english: And we do not raise claims on behalf of an inciter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the same ברייתא from steps 32-33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judges do not argue in defense of a מסית.

steps.title: Who mentioned a מסית at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the ברייתא never spoke about a מסית, so why bring him up?
steps.simpleTranslation: A מסית? Who mentioned him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's last line. Nothing earlier in it was about a מסית or about capital cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'we do not argue for a מסית' only make sense if there was an earlier rule that the court argues for other people. The ברייתא as written has no such rule, so the line looks out of place.

keyTerms.meaning: Who mentioned his name? (Nobody brought this up)

phrases.english: An inciter? Who mentioned his name!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of the line quoted in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's line about a מסית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא discussed money admissions, not capital cases or a מסית, so the exception has nothing to be an exception to.

steps.title: Words are missing from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is missing words. In money cases we don't argue 'he was joking' for him, in capital cases we do argue for the defendant, but not for a מסית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא is missing words, and this is what it teaches: if he did not claim he was joking, we do not claim it for him. In capital cases, even if he made no claim, we argue for him. But we do not argue for a מסית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by filling in the missing words of the ברייתא. Once they are added, the line about the מסית fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In money cases the defendant has to say 'I was joking' himself, or the court will not say it for him. In capital cases (דיני נפשות) the court looks for a defense even when the defendant offers none. The מסית is the one exception to that kindness.

keyTerms.meaning: The text is missing words
And this is what it teaches
Capital cases, where a life is at stake

steps.confusionAlert: The 'claim' in money cases is the specific 'I was joking' defense. The court will not suggest it if the borrower stays quiet, even though in capital cases it does argue for the defendant.

phrases.english: It is missing words
and this is what it teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא טָעַן, אֵין טוֹעֲנִין לוֹ.
phrases.english: If he did not claim, we do not claim for him.
phrases.notes: The claim here is 'I was joking' from the earlier steps.

phrases.english: But in capital cases,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא טָעַן, טוֹעֲנִין לוֹ.
phrases.english: even though he did not claim, we claim for him.
But we do not claim for an inciter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding missing words to the ברייתא (חסורי מיחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא jumps to a מסית with no connection to what came before.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא also contains a rule about capital cases, and the מסית is the exception to that rule.

steps.title: Why is a מסית different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a מסית loses the court's usual defense in capital cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about a מסית?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the exception. This sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the court works hard to save a defendant's life. The גמרא wants a source or reason for treating the מסית differently.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different?

phrases.english: What is different about an inciter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the exception stated in step 36.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason or source for not defending a מסית.

steps.title: The פסוק says not to spare or cover for him
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא בר חנינא, citing what he heard at רבי חייא בר אבא's lecture, says the Torah commands 'do not spare him and do not cover for him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא בר חנינא said: I heard at the lecture of רבי חייא בר אבא that a מסית is different, because the Torah says: 'Do not have pity and do not cover for him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק about the מסית. The Torah itself tells us not to shield him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Do not cover for him' means the court should not hide his guilt or hunt for ways to defend him. So the usual effort to save a defendant in capital cases does not apply to a מסית.

keyTerms.meaning: A public lecture or class
The Merciful One (ה׳, in the Torah)
Do not cover for him

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina said:

phrases.aramaic: מִפִּירְקֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא שְׁמִיעַ לִי,
phrases.english: I heard it at the lecture of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba:
an inciter is different, because the Merciful One said:
"Do not have pity, and do not cover for him."
phrases.notes: דברים 13:9

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 37.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'do not spare him and do not cover for him' removes the court's usual defense for a מסית.

steps.title: A second source: the first snake
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמן, quoting רבי יונתן, learns the rule from the נחש in גן עדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמן said in the name of רבי יונתן: How do we know we do not argue for a מסית? From the original snake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source for the same rule. This one comes from the story of the snake in גן עדן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The snake convinced חוה to sin, so he was the first מסית. How he was treated becomes the model for every מסית after him.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know?
The original snake (in גן עדן)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From where do we know that we do not claim for an inciter?
From the original snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the same rule taught in step 38.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule of not defending a מסית is learned from the original snake.

steps.title: The snake was not defended because he did not defend himself
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמלאי says the snake had many possible defenses but raised none, so ה׳ raised none for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי שמלאי said: The snake had many arguments he could have made, but he did not make them. And why did הקדוש ברוך הוא not make them for him? Because he did not make them himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבי יונתן's source with a teaching of רבי שמלאי about the snake's punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ did not argue for the snake, and the reason given is that the snake did not argue for himself. A judge would normally argue for a defendant in a life-and-death case, so the lesson is that a מסית gets no defense from the court; only his own claims count.

keyTerms.meaning: Arguments or claims in his defense
The Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.whatToRemember: In money cases the court won't raise the 'I was joking' claim for a defendant. In capital cases it argues for the defendant, except for a מסית. Two sources are given: the פסוק 'do not cover for him' and the snake, whom ה׳ did not defend because he did not defend himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how strict the Torah is with the מסית. The usual protections of a capital trial are taken away from him because of how dangerous his crime is.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Simlai said:

phrases.aramaic: הַרְבֵּה טְעָנוֹת הָיָה לוֹ לַנָּחָשׁ לִטְעוֹן,
phrases.english: The snake had many claims he could have made,
but he did not claim.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא טָעַן לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא?
phrases.english: And why did the Holy One, Blessed be He, not claim for him?
Because he himself did not claim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and supports the snake source given in step 39.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the court does not argue for a מסית
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי שמלאי's teaching that ה׳ did not argue for the snake because the snake did not argue for himself.

steps.title: What defense could the snake have used?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what argument the נחש could have made in his own defense.
steps.simpleTranslation: What could he have said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which defense the נחש could have used, since רבי שמלאי said he had defenses he never raised. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמלאי said only that the נחש had possible defenses. Here the גמרא wants one concrete example, so we can see what defense הקב"ה chose not to argue for him.

keyTerms.meaning: What could he have said? (what argument was open to him)

phrases.english: What could he have said?
phrases.notes: 'He' is the נחש. Which defense did he have that he never used?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the specific defense behind רבי שמלאי's general claim.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The actual argument the נחש could have raised to avoid blame.

steps.title: The teacher's words beat the student's words
steps.stepSummary: The נחש could have argued that אדם and חוה should have listened to הקב"ה (the Teacher), not to him (the student), so the sin was their fault.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the teacher says one thing and the student says another, whose words do we listen to? We listen to the teacher's words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the נחש could have said that the sin was not his fault. אדם and חוה had a clear command from הקב"ה, and they should have followed it instead of the נחש's advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a strong-sounding defense: whoever chooses to follow the lesser voice over the greater one is responsible for that choice. Still, הקב"ה did not argue it for the נחש. That is the source for the rule that we do not argue on behalf of a מסית.

keyTerms.meaning: The words of the teacher (here, הקב"ה)
The words of the student (here, the נחש)
We listen to / obey

steps.whatToRemember: The נחש had a real defense (people should obey the Teacher, not the student). Since הקב"ה did not argue it for him, we also don't argue for a מסית.
steps.confusionAlert: This argument does not mean the נחש was innocent. The point is that he had a possible defense, and it was deliberately not argued for him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This completes the source from the נחש for why בית דין does not look for defenses on behalf of a מסית, even in capital cases.

phrases.english: The words of the teacher and the words of the student:
phrases.notes: The Teacher is הקב"ה, who said not to eat. The student is the נחש, who said to eat.

phrases.english: whose words do we listen to?
We listen to the teacher's words.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּבְרֵי הָרַב וְדִבְרֵי תַּלְמִיד דִּבְרֵי מִי שׁוֹמְעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 41 and closes the derivation from the נחש.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The נחש could have said that אדם and חוה should have obeyed הקב"ה over him, so the blame was theirs.

steps.title: Whoever adds ends up subtracting
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה learns from חוה's words that adding to a command ends up weakening it, since she added 'do not touch it' to הקב"ה's command.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: Where do we learn that anyone who adds ends up subtracting? The פסוק says that חוה told the נחש: 'God said: Do not eat from it, and do not touch it.'
steps.whatsHappening: Staying with the story of the נחש and חוה, חזקיה teaches a new lesson: adding extra rules on your own can backfire. חוה added 'do not touch' to the command, but הקב"ה had only forbidden eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הקב"ה only forbade eating from the tree (בראשית 2:17). חוה reported a rule against touching it too. Once the touching turned out to be harmless, the real rule about eating also lost its force for her. So by adding, she ended up taking away.

keyTerms.meaning: Anyone who adds, subtracts (adding ends up weakening the original)
From where (do we learn this)?
Do not touch it (חוה's addition)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known principle: when a person reports a rule, he should say exactly what the rule is, and not mix his own extra additions in with it.

phrases.english: Ḥizkiyya said:
From where do we know that anyone who adds, subtracts?
As it says: "God said:
phrases.notes: בראשית 3:3. These are חוה's words to the נחש.

phrases.english: Do not eat from it,
and do not touch it."
phrases.notes: הקב"ה never said 'don't touch' (בראשית 2:17). חוה added that part herself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה מִנַּיִין שֶׁכׇּל הַמּוֹסִיף גּוֹרֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the נחש's defense to a new lesson drawn from the same story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Adding to something can end up taking away from it, as shown by חוה's added 'do not touch.'

steps.title: A second source: an extra letter in the ארון's measurement
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא brings another source for 'whoever adds, subtracts': the word אמתים, where an added letter א changes 200 into 2.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא said: We learn it from here: 'Two and a half אמות is its length.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא offers a different source for the same rule, taken from the measurements of the ארון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the א, the word would read מאתים, which means 200. Adding the letter א makes it אמתים, two אמות. So adding a letter made the number much smaller. This is the rule shown at the level of letters.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (introduces a different source)
Two אמות (cubits)
Two hundred (the word without the added א)

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiyya said: From here:
"Two and a half cubits is its length."
phrases.notes: שמות 25:10. Take away the א and it reads מאתים, which is 200. So the extra letter shrinks the number.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק as the source for חזקיה's rule.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 25:10: the added א turns מאתים (200) into אמתים (2).

steps.title: A third source: eleven curtains
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי brings a third source: in עשתי עשרה, an added letter ע turns twelve into eleven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: 'Eleven curtains.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers yet another source for the same rule, from the curtains of the משכן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the ע, the words would read שתי עשרה, which means twelve. Adding the letter ע makes it עשתי עשרה, eleven. Once again, adding something made the total smaller.

keyTerms.meaning: Eleven
Twelve (the words without the added ע)
Curtains (of the משכן)

steps.whatToRemember: There are three sources for כל המוסיף גורע: חוה's 'do not touch' (חזקיה), אמתים (רב משרשיא), and עשתי עשרה (רב אשי).

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
"Eleven curtains."
phrases.notes: שמות 26:7. Without the ע it reads שתי עשרה, which is twelve. The extra letter makes it eleven.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר עַשְׁתֵּי עֶשְׂרֵה יְרִיעֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third alternative source for the same rule.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 26:7: the added ע turns שתי עשרה (12) into עשתי עשרה (11).

steps.title: אביי limits the exemption to someone who says he was teasing
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the borrower is פטור only when he explains his earlier admission as 'I was teasing you.' He then starts to describe a different claim, which continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The rule that he is exempt was taught only where he says, 'I was teasing you.' But if he says...
steps.whatsHappening: אביי narrows an earlier ruling. A person who admitted a debt in front of hidden witnesses is פטור only if he says he was just joking. The line breaks off at 'But if he says,' so the גמרא is setting up a contrasting case that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase לא שנו אלא tells us the ruling has a limit. 'I was teasing you' does not deny that the words were said. It only explains that they were not a real admission. אביי is about to contrast this with a different kind of claim that may not get the same result.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They taught this only...' A formula that limits a ruling to a specific case
'I was teasing (joking with) you.' The borrower's explanation that his admission wasn't serious
'But.' It introduces the contrasting case

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think אביי is saying anyone who admitted a debt can always back out. He is limiting the exemption to the 'teasing' claim. The contrasting case is still coming.

phrases.english: Abaye says:
They taught [that he is exempt] only
phrases.notes: This is the case of someone who admitted a debt while hidden witnesses listened, then later denied it.

phrases.english: where he says: "I was teasing you."
But if he says:
phrases.notes: The sentence stops here. What he says comes on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the אגדה about adding to commands (steps 43-45) back to a monetary ruling about a denied admission. אביי limits that ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption for someone who admitted a debt in front of hidden witnesses applies only when he claims 'I was teasing you.' A contrasting claim is about to be introduced.
